summary: Requires securing messages exchanged between DHCP relay agents and servers. DHCPv4 had no guidance, and DHCPv6 recommended IPsec without requiring encryption. In light of pervasive monitoring concerns, it requires securing relay-to-relay and relay-to-server traffic for DHCPv6 and relay-to-server traffic for DHCPv4.

eli5.summary: The helpers that pass address requests along should use sealed envelopes so nobody can read or change them.

questions: how to secure dhcp relay messages
which ports do dhcp relays use
subtitle: DHCP relay agents and servers must be able to talk over encrypted IPsec, and operators are urged to turn it on.

tldr.problem: DHCPv4 gave no guidance on protecting messages between relay agents and servers, and DHCPv6 only said IPsec should be used, without recommending encryption. Those messages can carry sensitive client and relay information.
tldr.mechanism: Relay and server implementations must support IPsec in transport mode with ESP, using encryption. IKEv2 with pre-shared secrets should be supported for keys, and peers are identified by local configuration.
tldr.outcome: Support is required in implementations, but operators are only recommended to enable it. The hop-by-hop model leaves client-to-first-relay traffic unprotected.

today: RFC 8213 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2017, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Relay Traffic Needs Protection
sections.content:
A relay agent forwards DHCP messages between clients and servers. RFC 2131 (DHCPv4) and RFC 1542 (BOOTP) have no guidance on securing those messages. RFC 3315 (DHCPv6) says IPsec should be used, but does not recommend encryption.

With concerns about pervasive monitoring (RFC 7258), the RFC makes encryption a requirement for implementations: relay-to-server traffic for DHCPv4, and relay-to-relay and relay-to-server traffic for DHCPv6. The RFC says the document specifies optional requirements for relay agent and server implementations, and that it recommends operators enable the IPsec support.

The data at stake includes the DHCPv4 Relay Agent Information option (82), vendor-specific information and the Access-Network-Identifier option.
sections.eli5: Passing notes through several friends is risky if the notes are open. This RFC says to put the notes in a locked box first.

sections.title: What Implementations Must Support
sections.content:
Relay agents and servers MUST be able to exchange messages using the IPsec mechanisms of RFC 4301. For DHCPv6, the text of this RFC replaces Section 21.1 of RFC 3315 when it is followed.

If a client message goes through a chain of relay agents, each hop needs its own independent, pairwise trust relationship. If client C is relayed by agent A to agent B and then to the server, then A and B must use IPsec between them, and B and the server must use IPsec between them.

Operators are only recommended to enable IPsec; the requirement falls on implementations to support it.
sections.eli5: Every pair of neighbours in the chain has its own lock and key. A talks to B with one key, and B talks to the server with another.

sections.title: The IPsec Conditions
sections.content:
The RFC lists the conditions under which IPsec is used:

  • Selectors: relay agents are manually configured with the addresses to forward to, and the selectors are the address pairs and direction of exchange on DHCPv4 UDP port 67 or DHCPv6 UDP port 547.
  • Mode: transport mode with Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP).
  • Algorithms: combined mode, encryption and authentication algorithms as in Sections 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3 of RFC 7321. Encryption is required because relays may forward unencrypted client messages and sensitive extra information.
  • Security policy: messages MUST only be accepted from DHCP peers named in the local configuration.
  • Authentication: shared keys indexed to the source IP address of the received message are adequate.
sections.eli5: The rules say which mailboxes are allowed to talk, how the box is locked, and that you only open boxes from people on your list.

sections.title: Keys and Multicast
sections.content:
Relay agents and servers tend to be managed by one organization, so public key schemes MAY be optional. Manually configured keys may suffice but give no defense against replayed messages. So IKEv2 (RFC 7296) with pre-shared secrets SHOULD be supported, and IKEv2 with public keys MAY be supported. RFC 4107 has guidance on manual versus automated key management.

IPsec with multicast is more complex (RFC 5374), so relay agents SHOULD be configured to forward DHCP messages to unicast addresses.
sections.eli5: Swapping keys automatically is safer than writing one down and never changing it. Also, it is easier to lock a box meant for one person than one meant for a crowd.

sections.title: Limits of the Protection
sections.content:
The model is hop by hop. For DHCPv6 each hop between client and server must be secured; DHCPv4 has no support for multiple relays. Traffic between clients and the first-hop relay or server is not secured. Clients may follow RFC 7844 to limit what they expose, or use secure DHCPv6 (a work in progress when this RFC was published).

Manual keys, as noted in RFC 4552, cannot negotiate sequence numbers, so replay protection is not possible, and they tend to be long-lived, giving an attacker time to discover them.

Encrypted wire traffic does not protect data in servers, relays, databases, logs or backups, which also need securing. The approach also applies to Lightweight DHCPv6 Relay Agents (RFC 6221). The RFC makes no request of IANA.
sections.eli5: The locked box only protects the note while it travels between helpers. It does not help if someone steals the note from a helper's desk.
